title: Handle and see (Luke 24:36–43)
hookLine: he shows his hands and feet and eats a piece of broiled fish

cards: A room in Jerusalem, that same Sunday evening. The two from Emmaus have just burst in, out of breath, telling how they knew him in the breaking of bread. Everyone is talking at once.
And while they're still speaking, he is standing in the middle of them. Peace be to you. Nobody cheers.
Luke says they were troubled and frightened, and thought they were seeing a spirit. A ghost. Jesus answers their fear plainly, with his hands and with a piece of fish.

teach.h: TROUBLED: IT MUST BE A SPIRIT.
teach.b: He asks why they're troubled, and offers himself: "See my hands and feet, that it is I myself; handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me to have."
Handle, and see. The Greek verb means to feel with the hands, the way you'd feel for a light switch in the dark.
And still, Luke says, they didn't believe, for joy. Too happy to believe it. So he asks a very ordinary question: have you anything here to eat?
"And they offered him a piece of a broiled fish, and a honeycomb." He took it and ate it in front of them. A ghost doesn't eat fish.
It's a kitchen-table argument. Luke cares about bodies all the way through: a baby in a manger, a woman bent double, a servant's ear. He won't let the resurrection drift into a feeling or a memory.

The Catechism says the same in its own way: the risen Jesus is not a ghost; he invites touch and shares a meal, and his body is truly his own, the one that was crucified, though now in a new, glorified state.
That's why Catholics say in the Creed that they believe in the resurrection of the body. Not escaping the body. The body, raised.

how: Catholics hear Luke 24:35–48 on the Third Sunday of Easter in Year B of the Sunday cycle, and profess "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed.

games.q: you've come back from the dead, and your friends think you're a ghost. you've already shown them your hands. they still can't believe it. what do you do?
o: leave and let them work it out.
games.why: he asks if they have anything to eat. they give him broiled fish, and he eats it in front of them. a ghost doesn't eat fish.

practice: If something small is nearby, a bite of bread, a piece of fruit, a glass of water, take it slowly and notice the weight in your hand, the taste, the swallow; if not, just picture your next meal.
This body is alive, and it gets hungry, and that's not beneath faith. If you pray, give thanks for being alive in a body; if you don't, let the plain fact of eating be enough.

wordCard.voice: Broiled fish. What the risen Jesus ate in front of his frightened friends, proof that a spirit hath not flesh and bones. Today's word.
